chapter: Dance tastes, big bands and the boat
title: Young and middle-aged dance tastes, Dixieland versus big band, and rock and roll
summary: DeDroit says his Dixieland band played what it wanted, catered to collegians at the Forest Grill, used a big band for alumni dances, and shrugs at rock and roll.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: How about back in the 20s, did you notice a great difference between the music that the young people wanted, the style that they wanted, as opposed to the more middle aged people that catered to different tastes?

I'll tell you the truth. With a Dixieland band such as mine, we didn't worry about what they wanted. We played what we wanted. We were a Dixieland band, see? But when I went into the Forest Grill, I started getting the young college people, and I catered to them, so I would mix in a slow tune now and then. But they danced everything, you know? And I would say that the middle aged people went and moved for Tubi. Because when I used to play the alumni dances, then I had to load a band down.
But I wouldn't play them with a Dixieland band.

I'd play them with a big band, see? Because although you weren't getting the money, you had a song like Glenn Miller, you know, all the rest of them, you know. But I don't see much difference in the style of dancing, except young people, they don't dance.

No. They don't dance. And as far as rock and roll, I never did look at it, you know what I mean? The only concession I ever made was I let the rhythm play, because it didn't seem to have the, what I wanted, that circle, you know? So I wouldn't offer an opinion as an expert as a style of dancing, but I don't know, I got along fine with it.
